With all the recent subverses being banned, I started wondering about this issue. Is banning a subverse a violation of a user's freedom of speech? Can anyone really stand a chance in court against Internet censorship?
Is Internet censorship a constitutional violation?

The Constitution only prohibits the government from restricting speech, and even then there are limits, shouting fire in a theater, etc. No company, establishment, or organization is required to allow you to say whatever you want, whenever you want. You can absolutely throw someone out of your house for something they said, and Reddit, Facebook, Voat, etc have the same right.

There is no constitutionally protected free speech on a privately owned website. Nor should there be. Voat's right to do what it wills with it's property trumps someones right to say things Voat doesn't like. But you also have the right to go elsewhere. That's probably how you ended up on Voat in the first place. Another site pissed you off, and you came here.

If the government gets pissed off at something you say they have the forces to kill you or worse. The Constitution protects you from that force and limits government power. Voat doesn't have the power to force rendition you to a black site in Disappearastan and as a group of private citizens have rights of their own that supersede your ability to say what you want ON THEIR SITE.

Per the US Constitution? With the whole net neutrality thing that's a bit of a grey area. As common carriers, sort of, they are not supposed to limit access to the net other then illegal content, but there is no CONSTITUTIONAL right to free speech over a private network. The law may protect speech and content as a requirement of operating an ISP, but Comcast et al. have no constitutional limit on their ability to infringe. As I understand it.

In other words if you talk smack about Comcast on Voat and they sever your connection to the net they might be breaking the law, but they aren't violating the US Constitution.

Of course ISPs are regularly subpenaed by the Gubmint to provide records on users who say things people find objectionable and the ISPs comply usually with little complaint. So there's that can of worms for you.

That's a very country specific question. As Voat is a Swiss site, the hosting countries laws come into play as well as the country you're accessing from. Where as protection of free speech is, to some degree, a staple of western cultures, ISP regulations vary wildly. UK laws on ISPs are far different than Swiss, US, or Netherland laws. That's not an easy question to answer.

But, generally, ISPs don't filter unless the a government entity tells them to. That's a very loose generalization. The protection of that idea as a right is what the whole "Net Neutrality" argument is about. ISPs want to regulate based on financial gain where people see internet access as a fundamental right.
The government (whatever government you fall under) is the guarantor of your rights, not a company, not an individual.

The practicalities of providing a true internet platform that wholly embraces freedom of speech could only be accomplished by a site that is not owned by any one entity. We'd have to have some sort of "buy-in", where we all own the site, and its administration is handled by an elected board - similar to a credit union.

But, what would happen eventually is (and what happens in credit unions), by necessity, proxy voting becomes de rigeur, and our votes are under the control of a few people.

It would be an interesting experiment, but, it would end in bad blood, as certain people get frozen out, and certain people coalesce power.

Reddit & Voat are both for-profit corporations. We're playing in their sandbox, so they get to set the rules and can ban anyone they want for whatever reason. Basically, it's a business decision they're making about their product (us).

Constitutional freedom of speech protection only covers the government censoring you. To make this a constitutional case, you'd have to draw a line showing that Voat or Reddit were being coerced by government entities to delete/ban things they wouldn't have otherwise.

Like... what's the difference between chillstep and chilltrap. Drum n bass, liquid drum n bass and future bass... What makes these genres receive their names?
Can someone explain to me the different genres of EDM?

First of all, half of the "genres" you hear are made up on the spot by people, in my opinion. I've heard crazy things like "Summer chillstep deep house" to describe one song.

The idea is more or less how the rhythm progresses, the tempos, meter changes, intensity of the beats in the song, certain sound bytes in use, the structure of the melodies and harmonies, and the simple difference between dubstep, trap, D'n'B, house, trance, etc. etc.

So to answer you're question, the difference between chillstep and chilltrap is: one is a chill form of dubstep, one is a chill form of trap. Liquid drum and bass flows more than regular drum and bass, as generic D'n'B is very staccato and fast-paced, frantic. No idea what the hell future bass is.

It's hard to explain, because subgenres are often quite arbitrary. I've listened to a lot of electronic music but I can't tell the difference between for example, house, progressive house, deep house, tech house, etc.

In my opinion the best way to find out what a subgenre is, is to look it up and see what it's based on, if it's not obvious from the name of the genre.
